<reason>A opened strongly on enforceability and detector unfairness, but B executed the decisive narrowing: since determined cheaters evade both regimes, the policy is judged by what it does to obedient students, and "write the essay" and "show your prompts" are instructions that produce different products. A eventually conceded both defaults are honor codes, which collapsed its enforcement advantage into a contest over which instruction yields more skill. A's answer—that "process transparency" makes process the graded object so empty logs fail—rested on a reading of the motion B plausibly contested, and A never really rebutted B's point that annotating a machine-framed draft is editing rather than composing. A's "preference not to know" was memorable, but B's "knowing is not the good; practice is" met it head-on. B was more concise, answered A1/A2 directly, and made the vote easier; A also had a clipped opening. Close but real edge to B.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 ([B2.1]-[B2.4]) turning A's "fabrication cuts both ways" point into "then policy is decided by what it does to everyone else": for the conscientious, paperwork is behavior, so a permission default tells obedient students the draft is replaceable. This reframed the whole debate onto terrain A never fully recovered.</best_rebuttal>
